beginner: Cauliflower grows best in rich, well-drained soil with lots of compost worked in, and it needs steady, even moisture the whole way. More than most vegetables, cauliflower hates being stressed: if it dries out or runs short on food even briefly, it can quit growing and form a tiny, useless head early (called buttoning). Soil that holds moisture but still drains well is ideal.
seasoned: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder that demands a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at steady, even moisture. It is the fussiest of the cole crops: any check to growth from drought, low fertility, or a stalled transplant can trigger buttoning (premature, undersized curds), so the goal is uninterrupted, vigorous growth from set-out to harvest. Work in compost before planting and aim for a moisture-retentive but well-draining bed, since waterlogging invites root maggots and rots while drought stress ruins the curd. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground.

beginner: Cauliflower grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral (up toward 7.0) helps hold it back.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN and Iowa State both give 6 to 7; Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5). Cauliflower tolerates a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral.

beginner: Cauliflower needs rich soil and regular feeding to grow a good head. The big rule is to never let it get hungry or stressed: a plant that runs short on food or water stops growing and makes a tiny, useless head early. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about 3 to 4 weeks after planting out. Keep it growing steadily the whole way.
seasoned: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder, and steady fertility matters even more than with other cole crops because a hungry plant buttons, forming a tiny premature curd instead of a full one. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, using roughly 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate. Keep the plant growing vigorously and without interruption right up to curd formation; the most common cause of failed curds is any stall in growth from low fertility or uneven water. On acid or sandy soils, a boron and molybdenum deficiency can cause hollow stem and whiptail, so a soil rich in organic matter at a near-neutral pH is the best insurance.

beginner: Time to feed your cauliflower.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your cauliflower with nitrogen to keep it growing without a stall.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed a few weeks after planting out to keep it growing strong.
seasoned: High N to drive steady, uninterrupted growth to a full curd: a 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen feed beside the plants a few weeks after they go out.
seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about 1 pound of 33-0-0 (or roughly a half cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row) about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, watered in alongside the plants.

beginner: Cauliflower does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most cauliflower companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage-family pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the cauliflower fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate cauliflower from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids and caterpillars, two major cauliflower pests.
seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported cole-crop companions. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother cauliflower.
seasoned: Dill works for cauliflower mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and cabbageworms, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not shade the plants.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cole crops; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young cauliflower without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

beginner: Keep cauliflower away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, and kale. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting cauliflower shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and worst of all, caterpillars and their mess tucked down into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as the curd forms, larvae crawl into it and foul it, the costly damage that is very hard to clean from a tight white curd. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous cole-crop caterpillar in home gardens).

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants, chew the leaves, and crawl into the head you want to eat.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and contaminate the curd; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Cauliflower is a primary host for all three.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down. Tighten control as the curd forms, when contamination of the head is the expensive kind.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodges in the curd, where it contaminates the marketable product with insects and honeydew and is nearly impossible to clean from the tight florets. Curling and distortion of young leaves is common.

beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants and hide down in the curd, which is the part you eat.
seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested curd with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting. Pressure is heaviest on the long-season fall crop.

beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, ladybugs) that suppress this aphid.

beginner: Check the growing tips and the developing curd often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen once the curd forms, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
seasoned: Scout growing tips and the curd weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the head. Avoid excess nitrogen once the curd sets, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment, and a root-checked plant is also far likelier to button.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment, and a checked cauliflower seedling is prone to buttoning.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover, and a stunted cauliflower seedling often heads early and badly.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage without a growth check.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots. A clubroot-checked plant rarely makes a usable curd.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow cauliflower or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the curd.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the curd. Often the most serious cole-crop disease in warm, wet weather.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Small dark spots with rings like a target appear on the leaves and can spread onto the curd as brown, fuzzy patches that ruin it. It is worse in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Small dark leaf spots with concentric target-like rings and a yellow halo; in wet weather the spots enlarge, and on cauliflower the fungus can spread onto the curd as a brown, sometimes fuzzy discoloration that ruins its market quality. Clemson lists Alternaria brown spot among the main cauliflower diseases.

beginner: A fungus that spreads by spores in wet weather and on infected seed. It spots the leaves and, on cauliflower, can blemish the white curd, which makes it unsellable.
seasoned: Alternaria species (A. brassicae / A. brassicicola), fungi that spread by airborne and splashed spores and on infected seed; long leaf wetness and warm, humid weather favor them, and they survive in crop debris and on seed.

beginner: Remove badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry, and use a copper spray if it is spreading onto the curd. Keep water off the leaves.
seasoned: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow and let foliage dry, and apply a copper-based fungicide if the disease threatens the curd; control is largely preventive.

beginner: Start with clean seed, space plants for airflow, water at the soil rather than overhead, rotate away from cabbage-family crops, and clear away old plants where the fungus survives.
seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed, space for airflow, water at the soil line, rotate away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the curd.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors the leaves and can spot and darken the curd. Cauliflower's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: The curd develops soft, watery, brown or black mushy patches that quickly turn slimy and smell bad. It usually shows up in warm, wet weather on a curd that stayed wet.
seasoned: Soft, water-soaked brown to black lesions on the curd that rapidly become slimy and foul-smelling, the bacterial head rot Clemson lists for cauliflower; it spreads fastest in warm, wet weather and where water sits in a tied (blanched) head.

beginner: Bacteria get into the curd through small wounds or where water sits in the head, then rot it from the inside, especially in warm, humid weather.
seasoned: Soft-rot bacteria (Pectobacterium / Pseudomonas species) enter through wounds and natural openings and macerate the curd tissue; free moisture in the head and warm, humid conditions drive it, and a tightly tied blanch that traps water raises the risk.

beginner: There's no cure for a rotting curd, so remove affected heads. The fix is prevention: keep the curd dry and harvest promptly.
seasoned: There is no cure for a rotting curd; remove and discard affected heads. Management is cultural and preventive.

beginner: Keep water off the curd, give plants room so heads dry quickly after rain, blanch (tie the leaves) loosely so water doesn't pool, harvest promptly, and avoid bruising the heads.
seasoned: Keep the curd dry: space for airflow, blanch loosely so water drains rather than pools, avoid overhead watering and handling wet heads, harvest promptly once the curd is full, and do not bruise the heads.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Never let it dry out and wilt, since stress makes it head early and badly.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible; cauliflower must never go through a dry check, which triggers buttoning.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week (UMN: roughly 1 inch a week; USU: 1 to 2 inches, deep and infrequent), more in warm, dry spells while the plant is sizing up.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; cauliflower dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and crown rot in cold, wet ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves and stalled growth, and worst of all, a tiny head forms way too early (buttoning) because the dry spell stressed the plant.
seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then the classic failure: a stressed plant buttons, forming a tiny, premature curd instead of a full head. Drought stress is the single most common cause of a ruined cauliflower crop.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Cauliflower is fussy. If it dries out even once while young, it can make a tiny useless head instead of a full one. Keep it evenly damp from the beginning.
seasoned: Cauliflower is the least forgiving brassica: a single drought check, even on a young plant, can trigger buttoning, a tiny premature curd that never sizes up. Keep it evenly moist and unstressed from the start.

beginner: Keep the soil steadily damp as the plant grows. Letting it dry out at any point can ruin the head later.
seasoned: Hold unbroken even moisture as the frame builds; any drought stress along the way, not just at heading, sets up buttoning and a poor curd.

beginner: Keep the water steady while the white head forms. Any dry spell now makes it loose, grainy, or bitter.
seasoned: Even moisture from transplant all the way through curd formation drives a smooth, dense, white head. A single check here gives a loose, ricey, or bitter curd.

beginner: Keep watering evenly and cut the head while it is full but still tight and smooth.
seasoned: Keep even moisture and cut the head while the curd is full but still tight and smooth.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the plant never gets stressed. A cauliflower that dries out even once can make a tiny, premature head, so do not let it wilt.
seasoned: Even, uninterrupted moisture is the whole game with cauliflower: more than any other cole crop it punishes a dry check by buttoning, so the goal is steady, vigorous growth with no stress from transplant to harvest.

beginner: Keep the water steady the whole time, especially when the plant is young, so it never gets stressed into heading early.
seasoned: Even moisture matters from transplanting all the way through curd formation; a single drought stress at any point, but especially on a young plant, can trigger buttoning.

beginner: Cauliflower is best grown from transplants, since timing and a smooth, unstressed start are so important. For spring, start seeds indoors about a month before planting out and set the plants out around 2 weeks before your last frost; do not rush them into hard cold, since young cauliflower is touchier than cabbage. For fall, start them in early-to-mid summer. The key is to never let the seedlings get old, root-bound, or chilled, because that stress makes them head early. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.
seasoned: Cauliflower is almost always transplanted, since precise timing and an unstressed start matter so much. For spring, start seeds indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before set-out and transplant sturdy young plants out around 2 weeks before the last frost; cauliflower transplants are less cold-hardy than cabbage or broccoli, so do not rush them into hard cold. For fall, start indoors or direct sow in early-to-mid summer and set out so the curd matures in cool fall weather. The single biggest transplant mistake is setting out an old, root-bound, or cold-checked plant: that stress triggers buttoning, where the plant forms a tiny premature curd. Set out stocky plants with 4 to 6 true leaves, harden them off over 7 to 10 days, and keep them growing without a stall.

beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, and turnips.
seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, collards, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.

beginner: Don't plant cauliflower or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.
seasoned: Rotate so cauliflower and its brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present (UMN advises up to a 7-year break where clubroot is known). Repeated same-family cropping builds soil-borne clubroot, and holding soil pH near neutral also helps suppress it.

beginner: Cauliflower does not keep well at room temperature, only a day or two. It is best eaten soon after cutting or frozen.
seasoned: Cauliflower is a poor keeper at room temperature, holding only a day or two before the curd softens and discolors. Unlike cabbage, it is not a storage vegetable: plan to use it fresh or freeze it.

beginner: Store the head unwashed in the fridge crisper, where it keeps about a week (up to 2 to 3 weeks if very cold). Use it soon, since the curd yellows and starts to smell as it sits.
seasoned: Refrigerate the head unwashed, with a few wrapper leaves on, stem side down. It holds about a week in the crisper, and no more than 2 to 3 weeks even at an ideal 32°F and high humidity (Clemson; USU). The curd yellows and develops off odors as it ages, so use it promptly.

beginner: You can freeze cauliflower if you boil the florets briefly first (about 3 minutes), cool them in ice water, drain, and freeze; use them cooked. This freezer step is a different thing from the leaf-tying also called blanching out in the garden.
seasoned: Cauliflower freezes well after blanching: cut into florets, blanch about 3 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching (the boiling step) halts the enzymes that cause off-flavors; frozen cauliflower is best used cooked. Note this freezer blanch is unrelated to the in-garden leaf-tying also called blanching.

beginner: Cauliflower is not a keeper like cabbage. Cut it with a few leaves around the head to protect it, keep it cold, and use it within about a week, or freeze it for longer.
seasoned: Cauliflower is for fresh use or the freezer, not long storage; this is a real difference from cabbage, which keeps for months. Cut the head with a few wrapper leaves to protect the curd, keep it cold, and use it within a week or so. The curd discolors fastest in light and warmth, so refrigerate promptly.

beginner: Pick the type that fits your patience. For a first try, choose an easy self-blanching or self-wrapping kind like Snow Crown, Amazing, or Self Blanche, which need little or no leaf-tying. The colored kinds are fun and skip blanching completely: orange (Cheddar) and purple (Graffiti) just need full sun, and green Romanesco makes a beautiful spiraled head but takes a long, cool fall to do well.
seasoned: Match the variety to the season and your tolerance for fuss. For a first try, the early self-wrapping or self-blanching hybrids (Snow Crown, Amazing, Self Blanche) are the most forgiving and need the least leaf-tying. Open-pollinated whites (Early Snowball, Snowball Y Improved) are seed-saveable but want blanching. The colored types are the fun ones and skip blanching entirely: orange (Cheddar) and purple (Graffiti, Purple of Sicily) are grown in full sun for their color, and lime-green Romanesco (Veronica) brings a spiraled curd but wants a long, steady cool fall. Days-to-maturity figures are approximate and run from transplanting.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A rich, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer for steady feeding.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release balanced fertilizer; a single cauliflower in a pot is a heavy feeder in a small soil volume, and starving it is the fast track to buttoning.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather and keep the water steady. Cauliflower buttons (heads early) if it ever dries out, so this matters more than for most pot crops.

Transplant Oct 1 through Nov 15 and harvest from Dec 30 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Cauliflower follows broccoli's calendar here too: start seed indoors in late summer, transplant October into mid-November, and keep it cool and steady, since heat stress ruins curd quality. Skip planting cauliflower from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps it from growing well here.

beginner: In the Willamette Valley and around Puget Sound, start cauliflower seeds indoors in February and set plants out from April through early July, staggering plantings a couple of weeks apart for a steady supply of curds from early summer into fall. Right on the coast, OSU's guidance is more specific: plant in January, exploiting the coast's very mild winter, and again in June for a fall curd; there is no long continuous window there like the valley has. Keep cauliflower growing steadily with even water; a cold check or a dry spell can cause tiny, useless button curds instead of a full head.
seasoned: Cauliflower in the Willamette Valley gets a genuinely continuous window: start transplants indoors in February and set them out anywhere from April into mid-July, which supports staggered sowings for a spring curd and a fall one without needing a separate second planting. The immediate coast, per OSU's own numbers, is narrower and more specific: only January and June are marked as viable set-out times there, not a range. The January planting leans on the coast's exceptionally mild, marine-buffered winter, well ahead of the coast's own average last frost in late March; cauliflower transplants tolerate the coast's typically light frosts once hardened off. Neither zone needs a summer heat pause, but cauliflower is fussier than cabbage about steady growth: a cold check or moisture stress causes small, premature button curds rather than one good head, so keep it growing without a stall in either zone.

beginner: Cauliflower grows one dense, round head (the curd) in the center of the plant. There are white kinds plus fun orange, purple, and spiraled green Romanesco types, taking about 2 to 3 months to mature. It likes steady cool weather, so it is grown in spring and fall, not summer heat. Cauliflower is the trickiest of the cabbage family: it needs to grow without any stress, or it makes a tiny head early (buttoning) or a loose, discolored one. Many white types need blanching, where you tie the outer leaves over the head to keep it white. There are no side shoots like broccoli, so it is one head per plant, and it does not store like cabbage, so use it fresh or freeze it.
seasoned: Cauliflower is a cool-season brassica grown for the single dense white curd, the immature flower head, that forms at the center of the plant. It comes in white types plus orange, purple, and lime-green spiraled Romanesco forms, maturing from about 50 to 100 days, and is grown as a spring crop and a fall crop, timed to mature in cool weather. It is the fussiest of the common cole crops and less cold-hardy than cabbage or broccoli: the curd forms well only in steady cool weather around 60°F to 65°F, and almost any stress (heat, cold, drought, or a checked transplant) causes buttoning (a tiny premature curd) or ricing and discoloration of the head. Many white varieties need blanching, tying the outer leaves over the curd to keep it white, while self-blanching and colored types skip that step. Unlike broccoli it forms no side shoots, so it is a single harvest per plant, and unlike cabbage it does not store, so it is used fresh or frozen.

beginner: Your cauliflower is ready when the head is full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches), firm, and still tight, smooth, and white, usually a week or two after you tied the leaves over it. Cut the whole head off with a few leaves attached. Don't wait, because the head quickly goes loose and grainy and yellows. Use it within about a week, since it does not keep like cabbage.
seasoned: Cut the curd when it is full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches across), firm, compact, and still smooth and white, usually 1 to 2 weeks after blanching and roughly 50 to 100 days from transplanting depending on the variety. Slice the whole head off at the base with a few wrapper leaves to protect it. Harvest promptly: a curd left too long rices (separates into a loose, grainy surface), discolors, and starts to open toward flower, and that window is only a few days, shorter in warm weather. Refrigerate soon, since cauliflower does not hold in the garden the way cabbage does.

beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into a rich, well-drained bed and check that the soil is not too acidic. Try not to plant where you grew other cabbage-family crops in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases. Plan to water evenly and feed steadily, because cauliflower needs to grow without any stress or it heads early and badly.
seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained but moisture-retentive bed before planting and confirm pH is near 6.0 to 7.0, liming acidic ground well ahead where clubroot is a concern. Because clubroot builds in the soil, choose a bed where no cole crop has grown for at least 3 years. Set up to water evenly and plan for steady feeding, since the whole secret to cauliflower is uninterrupted growth with no stress, which is what prevents buttoning.
